The name “Murjiʾa” is connected with the history of the group’s emergence after the Battle of Ṣiffīn between ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya. When the Khārijites broke away from ʿAlī’s army because they rejected his acceptance of arbitration, they declared both ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya unbelievers. Most Muslims rejected this view. At that point, some argued that judgment on the matter should be “deferred” (irjāʾ) to God alone. In practice, this was a political position presented as neutrality. Those who held it therefore became known as the Murjiʾa. See al-Ashʿarī, Maqālāt al-Islāmiyyīn, Cairo, 1950, p. 197.↩︎
